transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi. Nice to meet you too. I came in because, well, my mind is just constantly jumping from one worry to the next. I work in a lab, and I keep stressing about whether our new partnership is going to end up cutting my position, or if my data is all wrong. 

Then it just spirals into worrying that my bills are going to pile up, or that my family thinks I'm falling behind. I even keep thinking I've already completely ruined my chances at grad school. It just never really stops.
Do you get unwanted thoughts that keep popping into your mind even when you try to push them away?

Yeah, they definitely do. I try to tell myself to just focus on one task, you know, like finishing a report or checking an assay at the lab. But it doesn't really work. One worry just sets off another one, and pretty soon I'm just staring at the screen while my head is running through every possible way things could go wrong.
Do you find yourself worrying about many different parts of your life, not just one specific problem?

Yeah, exactly. Like I mentioned when we first sat down, it really isn't just one thing. My mind is just constantly jumping around. It goes from work stuff—like if the lab's new partnership means I'll lose my job, or if my data is completely wrong—straight to my bills piling up. And then it's right on to personal things, like worrying my family thinks I'm falling behind, or that I've already ruined my chances for grad school. So, yeah, it definitely covers pretty much every part of my life.
Do you find yourself doing anything over and over, like checking, counting, or repeating things, to try to relieve these worries?

No, not really. I don't count things or... or have any routines like that. I mean, I double-check my measurements at the lab, but that's just normal work stuff. When it comes to the worries, it's really just all in my head. I don't physically do things over and over to try and make them stop, they just kind of stay stuck in my mind.
How long have you been feeling this constantly worried?

It's been about seven months now. It all started when the lab had a big shift in funding and they brought in a new commercial partnership. That completely changed how everything was being run, and I've just been feeling this way ever since.
When you start worrying, do you find it hard to stop or control the worry?

Yeah, it's really hard to stop. I try to tell myself to just focus on one task, you know, like finishing a report or checking an assay at work. But it doesn't work. One worry just sets off another one, and pretty soon I'm just staring at my computer screen while my head is running through every possible way things could go wrong. I can't seem to turn it off.
Have you been feeling down or depressed most days?
No, not really. I mean, I'm exhausted and stressed out all the time from the worrying, but I wouldn't say I feel sad or depressed. It's more just... I'm constantly on edge, rather than feeling down.
Do you feel these worries are mainly because of the changes at your lab?

I'm... I'm not really sure anymore. It definitely started with the lab changes, like that was the initial trigger. But now, it feels like it's about everything. It's not just work. I'll be at home worrying about my rent, or if my car is going to break down, or just... everyday stuff that never used to bother me. So I guess the lab set it off, but the worries aren't really just about that now.
Have you been feeling restless or keyed up?

Yeah, I'd say so. Especially at work, I just feel really wound up. Like, I can't even settle into my chair. I'm constantly tapping my foot or checking my messages. Sometimes I'll just walk back to the instrument room for no reason at all because I can't sit still. And I'm so on edge that even normal lab noises, like a centrifuge starting up or a door shutting, make me jump.
Do you feel your level of anxiety is much stronger than would be expected from the changes happening at your lab?

Yeah, definitely. I mean, the lab stuff is stressful, sure, but... it's just a job. The way I'm reacting, the way I'm worrying about literally everything now... it's way out of proportion. It's like my brain took that one stressor and just ran with it, and now everything feels like a disaster waiting to happen. So, yeah, it's definitely stronger than it should be.
